EXEMPT EMPLOYEE'S PAY IN THE FINAL (AND FIRST) WEEK OF EMPLOYMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Exempt Employee's Pay in the Final (and First) Week of Employment — Information Sheet is prepared in connection with the employment relationship between Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc., whose last day of work is stated here as October 1, 2026. Jordan Lee's stated weekly salary before termination is $1,500 per week, and the number of days actually worked during that final week is stated here as 3 of 5 scheduled workdays. It describes what the federal salary-basis regulation at 29 C.F.R. § 541.602 says about paying a salaried, overtime-exempt employee for a week of employment that starts or ends mid-week, the general full-week rule that provision is an exception to, how the California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual and a specific California statute (Labor Code § 515.7) each treat that federal test, and what the applicable Industrial Welfare Commission Wage Order separately does and does not adopt by reference. This information sheet does not itself determine whether Jordan Lee was properly classified as an exempt employee, whether Acme, Inc.'s payment for the week including October 1, 2026 satisfied the salary-basis requirement, or what amount, if any, is owed for that week.

GENERAL RULE: FULL SALARY FOR ANY WEEK IN WHICH ANY WORK IS PERFORMED
Under the federal regulation that defines what it means for an employee to be paid on a "salary basis" for purposes of the federal executive, administrative, and professional overtime exemptions, an employee is paid on a salary basis if the employee regularly receives, each pay period on a weekly or less frequent basis, a predetermined amount that is not subject to reduction because of variations in the quality or quantity of the work performed. Subject to specific exceptions, an exempt employee must receive the full salary for any week in which the employee performs any work, without regard to the number of days or hours worked, and an employer is not required to pay an exempt employee for a workweek in which the employee performs no work at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An employee will be considered to be paid on a “salary basis” within the meaning of this part if the employee regularly receives each pay period on a weekly, or less frequent basis, a predetermined amount constituting all or part of the employee's compensation, which amount is not subject to reduction because of variations in the quality or quantity of the work performed."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text), Code of Federal Regulations, general salary-basis definition (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-541/subpart-G/section-541.602)
  "Subject to the exceptions provided in paragraph (b) of this section, an exempt employee must receive the full salary for any week in which the employee performs any work without regard to the number of days or hours worked. Exempt employees need not be paid for any workweek in which they perform no work."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a)(1) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text), Code of Federal Regulations, full-salary-for-any-week-worked rule (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-541/subpart-G/section-541.602)
  Known gap: This is the general, full-week rule only; by its own terms it does not address what may happen in a week where the employment relationship itself begins or ends partway through — that specific situation is addressed by a separate exception described in this document's companion clauses. This clause quotes two subdivisions of a single federal regulation, 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a) and § 541.602(a)(1); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the eCFR page (fetched with two distinct User-Agent strings), and the two fetches differed only in a per-request CSP nonce value embedded in the page's script tags, not in the regulatory text itself.

EXCEPTION FOR THE INITIAL OR TERMINAL WEEK OF EMPLOYMENT
The salary-basis regulation carves out a specific exception to the full-week rule described above, applicable to the start or the end of an employment relationship. The regulation lists deductions that do not violate the salary-basis requirement, and one of those permitted deductions addresses this exact situation: an employer is not required to pay the full salary in the initial or terminal week of employment, and may instead pay a proportionate part of the employee's full salary for the time actually worked in the first and last week of employment, without losing the exemption for that week.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The prohibition against deductions from pay in the salary basis requirement is subject to the following exceptions:"
  — 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text), Code of Federal Regulations, introductory clause to the list of salary-basis exceptions (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-541/subpart-G/section-541.602)
  "An employer is not required to pay the full salary in the initial or terminal week of employment. Rather, an employer may pay a proportionate part of an employee's full salary for the time actually worked in the first and last week of employment. In such weeks, the payment of an hourly or daily equivalent of the employee's full salary for the time actually worked will meet the requirement."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(6) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text), Code of Federal Regulations, initial-or-terminal-week proration rule (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-541/subpart-G/section-541.602)
  Known gap: The regulation's own text does not define "week" for this purpose as necessarily aligned with a calendar week that includes the actual last calendar day worked — it speaks in terms of the "initial or terminal week of employment," which is ordinarily the employer's established workweek that happens to contain the first or last day of the employment relationship. This clause quotes one sentence group of 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(6); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the eCFR page (fetched with two distinct User-Agent strings), and the two fetches differed only in a per-request CSP nonce value, not in the regulatory text itself.

LIMIT: NOT FOR AN EMPLOYEE WHO WORKS ONLY OCCASIONAL, ISOLATED DAYS
That exception is narrow, and the same regulation immediately qualifies it. An individual is not paid on a salary basis if the person is employed only occasionally for a few days at a time and the employer pays a proportionate part of the weekly salary whenever so employed — that pattern describes casual or occasional employment rather than salaried employment, regardless of what portion of the weekly salary is paid. The initial-or-terminal-week exception applies only at the two edges of a single, ongoing employment relationship — its first week and its last week — not to some other week in which work happens to be performed on fewer than the usual number of days.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "However, employees are not paid on a salary basis within the meaning of these regulations if they are employed occasionally for a few days, and the employer pays them a proportionate part of the weekly salary when so employed."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(6) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text), Code of Federal Regulations, occasional-employment limitation (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-541/subpart-G/section-541.602)
  Known gap: The regulation's own text does not supply a bright-line test for how many consecutive weeks of full salary must occur before a relationship stops being "occasional employment for a few days" and becomes a genuine ongoing salaried relationship with a single terminal week; that line-drawing is left to the facts of a particular employment relationship. This clause quotes the sentence of 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(6) that continues directly after the sentences quoted in this document's companion clause; the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the eCFR page (fetched with two distinct User-Agent strings), and the two fetches differed only in a per-request CSP nonce value, not in the regulatory text itself.

HOW THE PROPORTIONATE AMOUNT MAY BE CALCULATED
The same regulation addresses how a permitted deduction under its list of exceptions — including the initial-or-terminal-week proration described above — may be calculated. An employer may use the hourly or daily equivalent of the employee's full weekly salary, or any other amount proportional to the time actually missed by the employee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "When calculating the amount of a deduction from pay allowed under paragraph (b) of this section, the employer may use the hourly or daily equivalent of the employee's full weekly salary or any other amount proportional to the time actually missed by the employee."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(c) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text), Code of Federal Regulations, method for calculating a permitted deduction (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-541/subpart-G/section-541.602)
  Known gap: This calculation-method provision applies to permitted salary-basis deductions generally, not solely to the initial-or-terminal-week exception; a second sentence of the same subdivision separately addresses the amount of a deduction imposed as a penalty for a major safety-rule violation under a different exception, 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(4), which is unrelated to the timing of a termination and is not addressed by this document. The regulation does not itself mandate the hourly method over the daily method, or specify how the number of scheduled workdays in a partial week is identified when an employee's schedule varies week to week. This clause quotes 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(c); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the eCFR page (fetched with two distinct User-Agent strings), and the two fetches differed only in a per-request CSP nonce value, not in the regulatory text itself.

WHAT THE CALIFORNIA WAGE ORDER'S INCORPORATION BY REFERENCE DOES NOT COVER
California's own overtime-exemption test for executive employees comes from Industrial Welfare Commission Wage Order No. 4-2001, not directly from the federal salary-basis regulation quoted elsewhere in this document. For the duties portion of the executive exemption, the wage order incorporates specific federal regulations by section number, as they existed on the date the wage order was issued. That incorporated list addresses only the duties test for the executive exemption — it does not include 29 C.F.R. § 541.602, the salary-basis regulation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "shall be construed in the same manner as such items are construed in the following regulations under the Fair Labor Standards Act effective as of the date of this order: 29 C.F.R. Sections 541.102, 541.104-111, and 541.115-116."
  — Cal. Code Regs. tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 1(A)(1)(e) (Industrial Welfare Commission Wage Order No. 4-2001, official PDF text), California Industrial Welfare Commission Wage Order No. 4-2001, Section 1(A)(1)(e), executive exemption (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the executive-exemption duties-test incorporation clause of Wage Order No. 4-2001; the same wage order's administrative- and professional-exemption provisions separately incorporate their own, similarly limited lists of federal duties-test section numbers that this document's own review of the wage order's text likewise found do not include § 541.602, but this clause does not separately quote those parallel provisions. The wage order's silence on § 541.602 does not, by itself, mean the salary-basis rule described in this document's other clauses fails to apply in California — only that the wage order's own incorporation-by-reference clause is not its source; this document's other clauses look instead to DLSE Enforcement Manual guidance and a direct statutory cross-reference for that. This clause quotes a single subdivision of Wage Order No. 4-2001; the source PDF was independently refetched with a second, distinct User-Agent string and confirmed byte-for-byte identical (matching MD5 checksum) to the first fetch.

DLSE'S STATED POLICY OF FOLLOWING THE FEDERAL SALARY-BASIS GUIDELINES
The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's own Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual states its general approach to the salary-basis test. Citing the California Supreme Court's instruction to compare the state and federal statutory schemes before giving weight to federal authority, the manual states that DLSE has concluded that the IWC intended enforcement of the salary requirement to follow the federal guidelines so far as possible, while certain federal guidelines may not be utilized in California because they conflict with California statutory law, case law, or public policy.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In making this determination for purposes of the salary basis test, DLSE has concluded that, to the extent possible, the IWC intended that the enforcement of the “salary” requirement was to follow the federal guidelines so far as possible; but that certain of the federal guidelines may not be utilized in California because they conflict with California statutory law, case law, or public policy."
  — DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 51.6.4 (rev. Dec. 2022), California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  Known gap: This is DLSE's own enforcement-guidance manual, not a statute or regulation, and a court is not bound to follow it. The quoted passage states DLSE's general orientation toward the federal salary-basis guidelines as a category; it does not, by itself, specifically confirm or reject the initial-or-terminal-week proration rule addressed in this document's other clauses. This document's own attempt to locate California case law specifically addressing 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(6)'s initial-or-terminal-week rule was blocked by CourtListener's free-tier daily search quota (HTTP 429, "Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") at the time of research, so no case law is cited anywhere in this document — only statutory, regulatory, and DLSE-manual sources are cited. This clause quotes a single passage of the manual; the source PDF was independently refetched with a second, distinct User-Agent string and confirmed byte-for-byte identical (matching MD5 checksum) to the first fetch.

DLSE'S MANUAL REPRODUCES THE SAME INITIAL-AND-TERMINAL-WEEK RULE
The same DLSE manual includes an appendix compiling the text of the federal salary-basis regulations that were in effect on July 1, 2000, under the section numbering the regulation used before a 2004 renumbering (former 29 C.F.R. § 541.118, now § 541.602). That reproduced text includes a subsection on initial and terminal weeks, stating that failure to pay the full salary in the initial or terminal week of employment is not considered inconsistent with the salary basis of payment, and that in such weeks, payment of a proportionate part of the employee's salary for the time actually worked will meet the requirement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Failure to pay the full salary in the initial or terminal week of employment is not considered inconsistent with the salary basis of payment. In such weeks the payment of a proportionate part of the employee's salary for the time actually worked will meet the requirement."
  — DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, Federal Regulations Appendix, reproducing former 29 C.F.R. § 541.118(c) (text current through June 20, 2000; 65 Fed. Reg. 38332), California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, Appendix compiling federal regulations in effect July 1, 2000 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  Known gap: This passage is a DLSE-compiled reproduction of the pre-2004 numbering of the federal salary-basis regulation (former § 541.118(c)), not an independent DLSE ruling. The manual's own introduction to this appendix states that only some of the reproduced federal text was adopted by the IWC for enforcement purposes, with inapplicable portions marked in strikeout and portions used for enforcement without further DLSE direction marked in italics; this document's PDF text-extraction process (character- and vector-level inspection of the underlying page) found no strikethrough line or italic font applied to this specific passage, but could not conclusively determine which of the manual's own marked categories, if any, the passage falls into. This clause therefore treats the quoted text only as confirmation that DLSE's own manual contains and reproduces a rule identical to the current federal one — not as an independent DLSE determination that the rule is binding on California employers beyond the current federal regulation quoted in this document's other clauses. This clause quotes one paragraph from the manual's appendix; the source PDF was independently refetched with a second, distinct User-Agent string and confirmed byte-for-byte identical (matching MD5 checksum) to the first fetch.

ONE DIRECT CALIFORNIA STATUTORY CROSS-REFERENCE: ADJUNCT FACULTY
At least one California statute expressly imports the federal salary-basis test by its current section number. Labor Code section 515.7, which extends the professional exemption to certain part-time faculty at independent institutions of higher education, requires — among other conditions — that the employee is paid on a salary basis as defined by 29 C.F.R. § 541.602, in addition to meeting one of the statute's own minimum compensation amounts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(2) The employee is paid on a salary basis, as defined by Section 541.602 of Title 29 of the Code of Federal Regulations, and receives one of the following minimum compensations:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515.7(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.7.)
  Known gap: Labor Code section 515.7 is narrow: by its own terms it applies only to an employee employed to provide instruction for a course or laboratory at an independent institution of higher education, not to exempt employees generally. This clause cites it only as a concrete example of a California statute directly incorporating 29 C.F.R. § 541.602 by its current section number — it is not a general California codification of the initial-or-terminal-week proration rule for the executive, administrative, and professional exemptions addressed in this document's other clauses, and this document's own review found no equivalent direct cross-reference to § 541.602 in Labor Code § 515 or in Wage Order No. 4-2001's own text. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Lab. Code § 515.7(a)(2)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page — the only differences between the two fetches were dynamic per-request JSF ViewState tokens and a timestamp-seeded debug function, not the statutory text — before being treated as verified.

The manual's own introduction to this appendix states that only some of the reproduced federal text was adopted by the IWC for enforcement purposes, with inapplicable portions marked in strikeout and portions used for enforcement without further DLSE direction marked in italics; this document's PDF text-extraction process (character- and vector-level inspection of the underlying page) found no strikethrough line or italic font applied to this specific passage, but could not conclusively determine which of the manual's own marked categories, if any, the passage falls into. This clause therefore treats the quoted text only as confirmation that DLSE's own manual contains and reproduces a rule identical to the current federal one — not as an independent DLSE determination that the rule is binding on California employers beyond the current federal regulation quoted in this document's other clauses. This clause quotes one paragraph from the manual's appendix; the source PDF was independently refetched with a second, distinct User-Agent string and confirmed byte-for-byte identical (matching MD5 checksum) to the first fetch.

expectedJSON.body: At least one California statute expressly imports the federal salary-basis test by its current section number. Labor Code section 515.7, which extends the professional exemption to certain part-time faculty at independent institutions of higher education, requires — among other conditions — that the employee is paid on a salary basis as defined by 29 C.F.R. § 541.602, in addition to meeting one of the statute's own minimum compensation amounts.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 515.7(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (2) The employee is paid on a salary basis, as defined by Section 541.602 of Title 29 of the Code of Federal Regulations, and receives one of the following minimum compensations:

expectedJSON.gap: Labor Code section 515.7 is narrow: by its own terms it applies only to an employee employed to provide instruction for a course or laboratory at an independent institution of higher education, not to exempt employees generally. This clause cites it only as a concrete example of a California statute directly incorporating 29 C.F.R. § 541.602 by its current section number — it is not a general California codification of the initial-or-terminal-week proration rule for the executive, administrative, and professional exemptions addressed in this document's other clauses, and this document's own review found no equivalent direct cross-reference to § 541.602 in Labor Code § 515 or in Wage Order No. 4-2001's own text. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Lab. Code § 515.7(a)(2)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page — the only differences between the two fetches were dynamic per-request JSF ViewState tokens and a timestamp-seeded debug function, not the statutory text — before being treated as verified.
